Hook: Seen from space at night, the Korean peninsula is one of the strangest sights on Earth. The south is a web of light. The north is almost dark, with one bright point where Pyongyang is. Here are the two halves' incomes per head, from the Maddison Project, on a log scale. Before the Second World War the peninsula was one Japanese colony, and in 1940 the north, with its mines, dams and heavy industry, was the richer half: about 2{,}624 dollars a head, against 1{,}975 in the south. After the division, the north stopped publishing figures that anyone could check, and there are no estimates for it from 1944 to 1989. By 1990 the south was more than five times richer. By 2022, 41{,}321 dollars against 1{,}569: a ratio of about 26 to one, between people who share a language, a history and, until 1945, a country.

Economists have argued for seventy years about what made the difference. The two halves chose different systems. The north planned its economy on the Soviet model. The south, after a poor decade, chose markets and exports, and a government that pushed its people to save. South Korea's investment rose from about 11 percent of its output in 1960 to about 41 percent by 1990: four of every ten won produced went into factories, machines, roads and houses. So did the south get rich by saving? Or is saving what a country does once it is getting rich for other reasons?

This part's question: can a country save its way to being rich? How much of growth comes from piling up capital, and how much from something else? Do poor countries, which have little capital, catch up with rich ones? And if capital is scarce where people are poor, and so should earn more there, why doesn't it flow to them?

In 1956 Robert Solow, at MIT, wrote down one equation for what capital can and cannot do. It says how capital per worker changes: by what is saved, less what is needed just to keep up. Its answer was uncomfortable. Saving can make a country richer, but not keep it growing. And a year later, when Solow measured America's growth with it, most of the growth came from something the model leaves out.
Economics, Built. Part twenty: growth, part one. Capital.

This part continues Act Five, the long run. You'll check Kaldor's facts of growth against the data, and see the knife edge that the first growth models stood on. Then you'll derive Solow's model, give the island a saving rate, and find the golden rule. You'll work out how fast an economy should converge, and ask whether poor countries do. You'll take growth apart into capital, labour and the residual, across time and across countries, and settle the argument over East Asia. And you'll let the island choose how much to save, put China in the model, and end with two dials, how forecasters use all this, and the frontier.
Kaldor: Chapter one. Kaldor's six facts, checked.

In 1961 Nicholas Kaldor listed six facts of growth that any theory would have to explain. Part three entered them on the series' list. Here they are, checked on the newest Penn World Table. One. Output per worker grows at a roughly steady rate: in the United States, about 1.6 percent a year since 1950, a little faster before 1985 than after. Two. Capital per worker grows too, at about the same rate, 1.5 percent. Three. The return on capital shows no trend: between about 6 and 10 percent a year for seventy years. Four. So the ratio of capital to output is roughly steady, between 3.2 and 3.9 years of output. Five. The shares of income are roughly steady: labour's was about 63 percent until 1980; since 2010 it has averaged about 59, the one fact that has slipped. And six. Growth rates differ enormously across countries. Over 1960 to 2019, across 91 countries, from minus 1.8 percent a year in COD to 6.2 percent in China.

So, sixty years on: the first four facts still describe the richest economy: output and capital per worker grow together at a steady rate, with a steady return and a steady ratio of one to the other. Economists call that a balanced growth path. The fifth held for decades and has slipped since about 2000; part thirty-nine asks why. And the sixth says that countries are not all on one path. The model in chapter three explains the first five in a single stroke. The sixth is harder, and it is what the rest of this part is about.
Harrod: Chapter two. Harrod, Domar and the planners.

Before Solow there was a simpler model, put forward by Roy Harrod in 1939 and Evsey Domar in 1946. It assumes every unit of output needs a fixed amount of capital: a capital-output ratio, v, of say three and a half years of output. Each year the saved share of output, s, becomes new capital, and a fraction delta of the old capital wears out. Put the two together and the growth rate is the saving rate divided by v, less depreciation. On the island, saving a fifth of output, the economy grows by 2.7 percent a year. More saving, more growth, for ever.

But there is a catch, and Harrod saw it. Workers need machines, and machines need workers, in a fixed proportion. The island's labour force grows by one percent a year. Save ten percent and capital barely grows. Each year there are more workers without machines to work: unemployment rises without limit. Save twenty percent and capital outruns the workers: machines stand idle, and idle machines earn nothing. Only one saving rate, 14 percent, the ratio times labour-force growth plus depreciation, keeps both fully used. Nothing in the model makes households save exactly that. Growth with full employment sits on a knife edge.

Knife edge or not, the model had one great attraction for planners: it turns a growth target into a number. To grow seven percent a year with a ratio of three and a half, a country must invest 35 percent of its output. If it saves only fifteen, the other twenty is a financing gap, to be filled by foreign aid and loans. Arithmetic of this kind ran through India's Second Five-Year Plan of 1956. Decades after economists had moved on, the international lenders were still using it. William Easterly found it in the 1990s in World Bank country reports, including one on Zambia that called the incremental capital-output ratio a useful, if simplistic, tool.

So Easterly tested it. Suppose, as the model does, that aid becomes investment one for one, and investment becomes growth a year later, with a capital-output ratio of three and a half. He ran the prediction for the countries that received aid from 1961 to the early nineties. Zambia got a great deal of aid. If the model were right, its income per head would have climbed to about twenty thousand dollars, the income of an industrial country. It fell to about six hundred. Across all the recipients, the correlation between the growth the model predicted and the growth that happened was slightly negative. Part of the failure is the fixed ratio itself. If capital and workers can be combined in different proportions, the knife edge disappears, and so does the promise that saving alone buys growth for ever. That is Solow's model.
Solow: Solow kept Harrod's saving and dropped the fixed ratio. The island now has capital: boats, nets, a granary, built from output that is saved instead of eaten. Output is made from capital, K, and labour, L, made more effective by technology, A, in a Cobb-Douglas production function, with capital's share alpha. Double both capital and effective labour and output doubles: constant returns. So everything can be measured per unit of effective labour: output per effective worker, y, is k to the alpha, where k is capital per effective worker. With alpha a third, each extra boat adds less than the last: equal steps in capital buy smaller and smaller steps in output.

Now the accumulation. Each year a share s of output is saved and becomes new capital, and a share delta of the old capital wears out. Capital per effective worker is a ratio, so its growth rate is capital's growth rate, less technology's, g, less the labour force's, n. Multiply through by k and you have the equation that runs the model: the change in capital per effective worker is investment, s times k to the alpha, less break-even investment, n plus g plus delta times k: what it takes just to equip new workers, keep up with technology and replace what wears out. The island saves fifteen percent; its people increase by one percent a year, technology by two, and five percent of its boats and nets wear out.

Here is the equation as a picture: Solow's diagram. Investment per effective worker is the saving rate times output: a curve that flattens, because of diminishing returns. Break-even investment is a straight line through the origin. Where investment is above the line, capital per effective worker grows. Where it is below, it shrinks. So from anywhere, the economy heads for the crossing, the steady state k star: the saving rate over the break-even rate, to the power one over one minus alpha. On the island, k star is 2.57, and output per effective worker 1.37; capital is about 1.9 years of output.

Now look back at Kaldor's list. In the steady state capital per effective worker stands still, so per actual worker, output grows at technology's rate g. So does capital per worker. The return on capital depends only on k, so it is constant. So is the ratio of capital to output. And with Cobb-Douglas production, competitive markets pay labour a share one minus alpha of income, whatever happens. Five facts in one stroke. The sixth, different growth rates, the model can produce only in two ways: countries on their way to a steady state, or countries with different technology. Hold on to that: the rest of the part tests both.

So what can saving do? Suppose the island doubles its saving rate, from fifteen to thirty percent. The investment curve doubles in height, and the steady state moves out: capital per effective worker 2.83 times as high, but output only 1.41 times. The elasticity of steady-state output with respect to saving is alpha over one minus alpha: with a capital share of a third, one half. And in the new steady state, output per worker again grows at g, two percent. Saving buys a higher level of income, not a faster rate of growth. Only technology keeps income growing. That is the uncomfortable answer.
PlayIt: Chapter four. Play it: how much should the island save?

Your turn. The island saves fifteen percent of its output and has settled at that rate's steady state. You may choose a new saving rate, to hold for the next hundred years. Which leaves the islanders the most to consume, per worker, in year one hundred? A, ten percent; B, twenty; C, thirty-three; D, fifty; or E, seventy. Remember that every fish saved to build a boat is a fish not eaten. Pause, and choose.

Here are the hundred years, computed. Each line is consumption per worker under a new saving rate, relative to staying at fifteen percent. Every higher rate starts with a cut: the islanders eat less to build more. Save seventy percent and consumption falls by more than half at once. Then the boats and nets pay off. Thirty-three percent overtakes the old rate after 14 years, and ends about 17 percent above it. Fifty percent takes 31 years to catch up and ends only 7 percent above, and seventy percent never catches up at all: the island is building more capital than is worth having. If you chose C, thirty-three percent, you found the best rate in the long run. It has a name.

It is the golden rule of accumulation, so named by Edmund Phelps in 1961, in a paper subtitled a fable for growthmen. In the steady state, consumption is output less what must be invested to stay there. Plot it against the saving rate: zero saving leaves no capital and little output; saving everything leaves nothing to eat. In between is a peak, where an extra unit of capital produces exactly what it costs to maintain: the marginal product of capital equals n plus g plus delta. With Cobb-Douglas production that happens when the saving rate equals capital's share, a third. Saving more than that is worse than wasteful. An economy above the golden rule could consume more now and in every future year, just by saving less. Economists call it dynamically inefficient.

One more experiment shows what saving can and cannot do. In year 10 the island doubles its saving rate, from 15 to 30 percent, and keeps it there. Growth jumps: income per worker grows by about 4.5 percent in the first year, more than twice its usual rate. Half of the eventual gain arrives within 10 years. Then growth slides back to two percent, technology's rate, where it stays. What is left is a level: income about 41 percent higher than it would have been, for ever. A country can save its way to being richer. It cannot save its way to growing faster for ever.
Transition: Chapter five. How fast does an economy converge?

If an economy is below its steady state, how fast does it get there? Divide the Solow equation by k: the growth rate of capital per effective worker is the saving rate times the average product of capital, less the break-even rate. Near the steady state, a first-order expansion in the log of k turns this into a simple rule. The gap between log output and its steady state shrinks exponentially, at a rate lambda equal to one minus alpha, times n plus g plus delta. Each year, the same share of the remaining gap is closed. On the island, two thirds of eight percent: 5.3 percent a year, so half of any gap closes in about 13 years.

Here is the exact path, simulated year by year, for an island that starts with a quarter of its steady-state capital. With capital's share at a third, half of the gap in output is gone in 10 years, a little faster than the rule's thirteen, because far from the steady state capital is scarce and earns more. Within a generation the island is nearly there. Now suppose capital's share were much larger, three quarters, as it would be if capital meant not only boats but the skills of the people who use them. Diminishing returns set in more slowly, and lambda falls to 2 percent: half the gap closes in about 35 years.

That is the model's prediction, and it can be checked. With capital's share at a third, the textbook says about five percent a year. When economists in the early 1990s measured how fast countries closed their gaps, they kept finding about two percent, so often that Robert Barro later called it an iron law. Mankiw, Romer and Weil's estimate was 1.4 percent. Two percent fits the model only if capital's share is about three quarters, far above the third that the national accounts pay to capital. To see how those numbers were found, and whether poor countries catch up at all, we need the data.
Convergence: Chapter six. Do poor countries catch up?

If every country had the same steady state, the Solow model would make a sharp prediction: the further below it a country starts, the faster it grows. Poor countries would catch up. Here are 89 countries with a million people or more, each placed by its income per head in 1960 and its growth over the next thirty years. If anything, the line slopes up: richer countries grew a little faster. Over those decades the poor did not catch up, they fell further behind. Lant Pritchett summed up two centuries of it in the title of a 1997 paper: divergence, big time.

But the model does not say all countries have the same steady state. A country that saves little, whose population grows fast, or whose people have little schooling, should be heading for a lower one. Robert Barro's answer, in 1991, was to compare countries holding those things fixed. On the left, sixty years of the newest data with no controls: almost no slope. Rich and poor grew at about the same rate on average. On the right, the same growth and the same starting incomes, each net of the country's investment rate, population growth and schooling in 1960. Now the line slopes down clearly. Among countries with similar saving, population growth and schooling, the poorer grew faster. The slope implies that each country closed about 1.3 percent of the gap to its own steady state each year: a half-life of about 55 years. That is conditional convergence.

The most famous test came a year later. Gregory Mankiw, David Romer and David Weil took the steady state itself to the data: log income should rise with the log of the saving rate and fall with the log of population growth plus g plus delta, with matching coefficients alpha over one minus alpha. Across ninety-eight countries, saving and population growth alone explained 59 percent of the differences in income. But the coefficients implied a capital share of about 0.59, twice the national accounts' third. So they added human capital, accumulated like physical capital, with the share of the working-age population in secondary school as its saving rate. Now physical capital's share came out at 0.31, human capital's at 0.28, and the model explained 78 percent of the variation. Broad capital, the two together, has a share near three fifths. And countries converged at about 1.4 percent a year: slower than the textbook, as a large broad share says it should be.

The controls are only what can be measured. Each country may have its own steady state, set by its institutions, geography or culture. In 1995 Nazrul Islam cut the same data into five-year panels and gave every country its own constant. The speed of convergence jumped to about 5 percent a year, close to the textbook's. That is not a contradiction: now each country is converging to its own level, not to one predicted from its saving and schooling. Panels this short have a bias of their own: with a constant for every country, the estimated speed is pushed upward, as Stephen Nickell showed in 1981, so the truth may lie between. And Danny Quah argued that the world is not converging to one distribution but splitting into clubs: twin peaks of the rich and the poor. Conditional convergence is a fact. Whether the poor catch up is another question.

That goes on the list of facts. Poor countries grow faster than rich ones once saving and schooling are held fixed, and not otherwise. The data column: about 1.3 percent a year with the controls, nothing without them. And Agora's column is filled by the model of this part: an economy below its own steady state grows faster the further below it starts.
Accounting: Chapter seven. Growth accounting: Solow's residual.

The model also gives a way to take growth apart. Write output as technology, A, times capital to the alpha, times hours worked, made more skilled by human capital h, to the one minus alpha. Take logs and differentiate with time, and output's growth rate is the sum of capital's growth weighted by alpha, the growth of hours and skills weighted by one minus alpha, and the growth of A. Everything except A can be measured. So A's growth is what is left over: the residual, also called total factor productivity. The weight alpha comes from the national accounts: under competition, it is capital's share of income.

Solow did exactly this in 1957, for the United States. Between 1909 and 1949, output per man-hour in the private non-farm economy doubled. More capital per worker accounted for an eighth of the increase. The other seven eighths, 87.5 percent, he attributed to technical change in the broadest sense: anything that shifts the production function. Moses Abramovitz, who had found much the same a year earlier, called the residual some sort of measure of our ignorance about the causes of growth. A critic who checked Solow's arithmetic found a slip; corrected, the share came to ninety percent.

Here is the same accounting on the Penn World Table, for the United States from 1950 to 2019, per hour worked. Output per hour grew by 1.86 percent a year. More capital per hour contributed 0.61 points, and more schooling 0.33. The residual: 0.91 points, about 49 percent. Measured schooling has eaten into Solow's seven eighths, but half of growth is still unexplained by the inputs. And the residual is not steady. It grew by 1.3 percent a year until 1973, by half a percent from 1973 to 1995, by 1.5 percent in the decade of the internet's spread, and by half a percent again since 2005.

Now eight countries, each over the longest span the table covers well. In the rich countries the residual is between about 28 and 49 percent of the growth of output per hour. South Korea's output per hour grew 5.5 percent a year from 1966; more than half of that was more capital. China's grew by 7.7 percent from 1980, with a residual of 3.4 percent, the largest here. And in Brazil and Nigeria the residual is about zero or below: all their growth came from accumulating, and output per hour grew slowly for countries so far behind. A country can pile up capital and still fail to use it better.

What is in the residual? Technology, in the sense of new ideas and new machines. Organization: better management of the same inputs. Reallocation: a worker who moves from a farm to a factory produces more without any new capital. And mismeasurement. In 1967 Dale Jorgenson and Zvi Griliches argued that if the quality of capital and labour were measured properly, most of the residual would disappear. Better measurement has since shrunk it, but not to zero. The next part builds a model of the biggest item, ideas.
EastAsia: Chapter eight. East Asia: perspiration or inspiration?

The argument over East Asia began with another economy. In the 1950s and 1960s the Soviet Union grew fast: income per head by about 3.3 percent a year, by the Maddison Project's reckoning, and it was closing the gap with America. Its planners did it by force of accumulation: very high investment, and millions moved from farms into factories. Then growth slowed, to 1.4 percent in the 1970s and 0.7 in the 1980s. Soviet income per head never passed about 38 percent of America's. Diminishing returns, with a small residual, is exactly what Solow's model says such growth runs into.

Many economists extrapolated. The best-selling textbook of the age, Paul Samuelson's Economics, showed in its 1961 edition Soviet national income overtaking America's between 1984 and 1997, on the growth rates it assumed. The 1980 edition still drew the crossing, now between 2002 and 2012. The forecast rested on carrying past growth into the future at its past rate. What happened: Soviet growth slowed decade by decade, and the Soviet Union dissolved in 1991 without overtaking. Called it? Wrong. The economists David Levy and Sandra Peart traced the forecast through the editions.

In 1994 Paul Krugman applied the same reasoning to East Asia, in an essay called The Myth of Asia's Miracle. Its evidence came from Alwyn Young, who had measured the four tigers' inputs with unusual care: hours, schooling, the entry of women into paid work, and capital by type of asset. Hong Kong's residual: about 2.3 percent a year. Singapore's: 0.2. South Korea's: 1.7, and Taiwan's 2.6, outside agriculture. Respectable numbers, but no better than many slower-growing economies in the OECD or Latin America. The miracle was in the inputs. The same accounting on the Penn World Table, with its own inputs, tells a similar story: Singapore grew by 8.7 percent a year from 1966 to 1990, and capital alone accounts for 6.0 points of it. Its residual is 0.5.

The verdict was challenged. Chang-Tai Hsieh measured the residual a second way, from prices rather than quantities. If output per unit of input is rising, the inputs' prices must be rising on average too: the residual is the share-weighted growth of the rental rate of capital and the wage. If capital had piled up as fast as Singapore's national accounts say, with so little productivity growth, its return should have collapsed. It did not. Hsieh's price-based residual for Singapore is more than two points a year higher than the quantity-based one. For Taiwan about one point; for Korea and Hong Kong the two methods roughly agree. Both methods rest on the same identity, so one of the data sets is wrong: Singapore's investment figures, or its interest rates. The argument became one about measurement.

What should we make of it? Perspiration is not a slur. Saving forty percent of output, keeping children in school and bringing women into paid work are real achievements, and they made tens of millions of people rich. But growth that comes from piling up inputs slows as the inputs run into diminishing returns. South Korea's income per head grew by about 8 percent a year in the 1980s, 4 in the 2000s and 2 in the 2010s, as it neared the frontier. Unlike the Soviet Union, it got there first. That is the difference the residual makes.
Levels: Chapter nine. Development accounting: why levels differ.

Growth accounting splits growth over time. Development accounting splits levels across countries. Income per worker is productivity times capital per worker to the alpha, times human capital per worker to the one minus alpha. Robert Hall and Charles Jones rewrote it with the capital-output ratio instead of capital per worker. Then income is the product of three factors: capital intensity, schooling and productivity. Why the rewrite? In the Solow model a country with higher productivity also builds more capital, so capital per worker partly reflects productivity. The ratio of capital to output does not, so the extra capital that productivity induces is credited to productivity.

Hall and Jones did it for a hundred and twenty-seven countries in 1988. Output per worker in the five richest countries was 31.7 times that in the five poorest. Capital intensity accounts for a factor of 1.8. Schooling, a factor of 2.2. Productivity, a factor of 8.3. With no differences in productivity, the richest countries would have been only about four times richer than the poorest, not thirty.

Here is the same accounting for 2019, on the newest Penn World Table. Each country is placed by its output per worker, relative to the United States. In gold, its capital intensity times schooling. They rise with income, but gently: the gold cloud is flat. In pink, productivity. It rises almost one for one with income. Between the ninetieth and tenth percentiles, output per worker differs 15 times; capital and schooling together, about 3 times; productivity about 7 times. Francesco Caselli's summary is the share of the variance of log income that the factors alone would produce if every country had America's productivity. In 1996 data he found between 0.26 and 0.40, depending on the form. In 2019 it is lower still: 0.16 and 0.30. Capital and schooling explain well under half of why some countries are rich.

Six countries, each relative to the United States. Read across India's row. Its output per worker is 0.14 of America's. Its capital intensity is 1.07: India has about as much capital per unit of output as America. Its schooling factor is 0.58. And its productivity is 0.23. Multiply the three and you get its income. The pattern holds down the table: capital intensity close to one everywhere, schooling lower, and productivity lowest of all. Poor countries are not mainly short of capital. They get less out of everything they have. Why, is the subject of the next part.
Lucas: Chapter ten. Why doesn't capital flow to poor countries?

In 1990 Robert Lucas asked a question that the Solow model makes hard to answer. If two countries share a technology, the one with less capital per worker has the higher marginal product of capital, and the return falls with income in a precise way. So the ratio of returns depends only on the ratio of incomes. In his data American income per worker was fifteen times India's. With capital's share at 0.4, capital should have earned about 58 times as much in India. Every dollar of new investment in the world should have gone to India and countries like it. It did not.

Lucas offered answers himself. Start from fifty-eight. First, workers are not equal. Using Anne Krueger's estimates, he supposed an American worker was worth about five Indian workers in human capital. Then income per effective worker differs only threefold, and the ratio of returns falls to about 5. Second, if each worker's productivity also rises with the skills of those around them, as in his own model of 1988, the gap vanishes: about one. He also named risk: of default, of expropriation, and the imperfections of capital markets. The puzzle has, if anything, deepened. In the 2000s, Eswar Prasad, Raghuram Rajan and Arvind Subramanian showed, net capital often flowed uphill, from poorer countries to richer ones.

Redo the calculation with 2019 data. India has grown fast, and American output per worker is now about 7 times India's. With the same technology, capital should earn about 19 times as much in India. Allow for schooling, and the prediction is about 8 times. The Penn World Table also estimates what capital actually earns, from national accounts: about 12 percent a year in India and 8 in America. A ratio of 1.5. Returns are higher in India, but nothing like the model's prediction, which means that the model's premise, the same A, is wrong. The answer to Lucas's question is the same as the answer to the last chapter's: productivity differs.
Ramsey: Chapter eleven. Ramsey's problem: saving chosen.

Solow took the saving rate as given. In 1928, nearly thirty years earlier, the young Cambridge mathematician Frank Ramsey had asked how much a nation ought to save. The islanders choose a path of consumption to maximize the discounted sum of their utility, for ever. Written per effective worker, the discount rate beta is impatience, rho, less the growth of the population and an allowance for technology. subject to the same accumulation as before: what is not eaten becomes capital. Ramsey himself refused to discount the future. To do so, he wrote, is a practice which is ethically indefensible and arises merely from the weakness of the imagination. David Cass and Tjalling Koopmans, in 1965, put the discount rate back, and the model now carries all three names.

The tool is the Hamiltonian, the dynamic version of a Lagrangian. It adds to today's utility the value of today's addition to capital, with mu the shadow value of a unit of capital. Choosing consumption: eat until the marginal utility of consumption equals the value of capital. The shadow value then changes over time at the rate of the discount rate, less what capital earns. Differentiate the first condition, substitute beta, and out comes the Euler equation of part seven, now with production in it. Consumption per effective worker grows when the net return on capital exceeds the rate of impatience plus theta times technology's growth, and shrinks when it falls short.

Two equations, two variables: draw them in the plane of capital and consumption. Capital stands still along a hump: consumption equal to output less break-even investment. Its peak is the golden rule. Above the hump capital shrinks; below it, capital grows. Consumption stands still along a vertical line, where the marginal product of capital just covers depreciation, impatience and growth. To its left consumption rises; to its right it falls. Where they cross is the steady state. The arrows show the trouble. Almost every starting point runs away: towards no capital at all, or towards too much capital and nothing to eat.

Only one path leads to the steady state, the saddle path, and the islanders must jump onto it. Agora finds it by shooting. Start with half the steady state's capital. Guess a level of consumption, and integrate the two equations forward. Guess six percent too high, and the islanders eat their capital: the path curls left and runs out. Six percent too low, and they overshoot, piling up capital they will never eat. The right guess lies between, so bisect: halve the interval, see which way the path misses, and repeat. After eighty halvings, consumption starts at 0.951, and the path rides into the steady state.

What does the island choose? In the steady state the Euler equation says the interest rate, the net marginal product of capital, equals impatience plus theta times growth: the modified golden rule. With these parameters, the interest rate is 7 percent. Capital per effective worker settles at 4.63, well short of the golden rule's 8.51. The islanders save about 22 percent, not a third. Because they are impatient, they stop short of the consumption-maximizing capital stock, and an optimizing economy can never overshoot it into dynamic inefficiency. The same machinery, with the climate added, is how economists put a price on carbon.
China: Chapter twelve. China's growth in the model.

No economy has tested the model harder than China's since its reforms began in 1978. It invested about 36 percent of its output in 1978, and at the peak, in 2011, about 47 percent, measured at international prices. So its capital grew faster than its output: from about 3.4 years of output to 5.5. Diminishing returns say that so much accumulation should drive the return on capital down. For fifteen years it did the opposite: the return rose, through the 1980s and into the 1990s. Only later did it fall.

Take China's growth apart, period by period. From 1980 to 1995, output per hour grew 7.4 percent a year, and more than half of it was the residual, 4.1 percent: farms freed from collectives, workers moving from fields to factories, firms allowed to compete. From 1995 to 2008, output per hour grew faster still, and capital deepening took a larger share. After 2008, output per hour still grew fast, but capital deepening now did most of the work, and the residual fell to 2.2 percent. That is what growth that runs into diminishing returns looks like.

How can capital pile up without its return falling? Zheng Song, Kjetil Storesletten and Fabrizio Zilibotti built a model of China with two kinds of firm. State firms have poor productivity but easy access to the banks. Private firms are more productive, but must finance themselves. As workers move from state firms to private ones, measured productivity rises, and capital keeps earning a high return even as it accumulates. Private entrepreneurs save hard to grow, and the deposits the banks collect, with few private borrowers to lend to, flow abroad. One mechanism, reallocation, accounts for high growth, a high return and a growing trade surplus at the same time. It is the residual of chapter seven, given a cause.

What does the model say about China's future? Reallocation runs out once the state firms have shed their workers. An investment rate near half of output is far above the golden rule's third: more capital now adds little to consumption. So growth must come from the residual, or it will slow, as Korea's did and the Soviet Union's did. How much productivity is still to be gained by moving capital and workers to better uses is a dial this series opened in part nine, and returns to in part twenty-one.
Dials: Chapter thirteen. The Dials: how fast, and how much capital?

This part opens a dial: how fast do economies close the gap to their steady states? Mankiw, Romer and Weil: 1.4 percent a year across ninety-eight countries, and 2.0 percent among the rich ones, holding saving, population growth and schooling fixed. Islam's panels, with a constant for each country: about 5 percent. This film's own estimate, on sixty years of the newest data, with the same controls: about 1.3 percent, with a wide interval. And Kremer, Willis and You's unconditional convergence since 2005, with no controls at all: about 0.7 percent. The status: contested. Cross sections say one to two percent, panels say five or more, and the gap between them is a question of what each country is converging to.

What the range means is easier to see as half-lives. At one and a half percent a year, a quarter of any gap is still there after ninety years. At five percent, half the gap closes in fourteen years, and within a lifetime the gap is gone. Whether poverty is a matter of generations or of centuries depends on which end of the dial is right. This film's 1.3 percent sits with the cross sections.

The second dial was opened in part eight: capital's share, the alpha that has run through this whole part. Cobb and Douglas's regression, Gollin's corrected labour shares, and the Penn World Table all put it between about 0.23 and 0.38. This part adds one row: Mankiw, Romer and Weil's augmented regression, 0.31 for physical capital, with human capital's 0.28 beside it. The status stays settled within a range, for physical capital. The American labour share since 1950 puts it at about 0.38. But the speed of convergence in the data fits a broad share, physical and human capital together, of three fifths or more: the dial depends on what you count as capital.
Practice: Chapter fourteen. In practice: potential output and the long-term budget.

This part's model is at work every year in budget offices. The Congressional Budget Office describes its estimate of potential output, the economy's output at full employment, as built on a Solow growth model. Output's growth is the share-weighted growth of capital and labour, plus the residual. On a balanced path capital grows as fast as output, so the residual counts more than once: output grows at the rate of hours plus the residual divided by one minus alpha. Suppose hours grow by 0.4 percent a year, an assumption for the arithmetic. If the residual grows as it did from 2005 to 2019, potential growth is about 1.2 percent a year. If it grows as it did on average since 1950, about 1.9. Half a point of the residual, and the whole budget outlook, ride on a number the model does not explain.

The second use is the long-term budget. Debt as a share of output evolves with the interest rate, r, and the growth rate, g. Each year the ratio is multiplied by one plus r over one plus g, and the primary deficit is added. If the interest rate exceeds growth, debt grows of itself unless the government runs surpluses. If growth exceeds the interest rate, as it did for most of the 2010s, a debt ratio can fall without any surplus, a point Olivier Blanchard made in his presidential address of 2019. The growth models say which is normal. In Ramsey's economy the interest rate is impatience plus theta times growth, above growth; an economy with r below g for ever would be saving beyond the golden rule. Andrew Abel, Gregory Mankiw, Lawrence Summers and Richard Zeckhauser proposed a test that does not need the interest rate: an economy is not over-saving if what capital earns exceeds what is invested, year after year. By that test, they found, the United States and the other large economies are not.

Who does this work? Budget offices, for potential output and the long-term projections. Central banks, for the output gap and the neutral rate of interest, which part thirty takes up. The IMF and the World Bank, which project medium-term growth for every member country, and, as Easterly showed, have not always used the best model to do it. And long-horizon investors, for whom a growth rate is the main input to what stocks and bonds will pay.
Outro: So: can a country save its way to being rich? Richer, yes. Saving raises the level of income, and East Asia's saving and schooling were real achievements. Growing faster for ever, no. Diminishing returns bring growth back to the rate of technology, as the Soviet Union found, and, more gently, South Korea. Across countries, capital and schooling explain less than half of the gap between rich and poor. The rest is productivity: the residual this model leaves out.

Part twenty in twelve lines. The two Koreas: one people, two systems, and a ratio of twenty-six to one. Kaldor's facts still hold, except labour's share. Harrod and Domar's model stood on a knife edge, and its financing gap failed Easterly's test. Solow's model says saving sets the level of income, and only technology sets its long-run growth. The golden rule is to save capital's share, and doubling the island's saving raised its income by about 41 percent, for good. The textbook's speed of convergence is five percent a year; the data say one or two. Countries converge once saving and schooling are held fixed, and until about 2000 not otherwise. The residual is about 49 percent of America's growth per hour. East Asia grew mostly by accumulation. Capital and schooling explain well under half of income differences. Capital should earn fifty-eight times as much in India, and earns about one and a half. And Ramsey's choice of saving, China, two dials, potential output, and convergence at last.

The problems. The Solow steady state; the golden rule; levels, not growth; the speed of convergence; growth accounting; development accounting; Lucas's calculation; and a starred problem on Ramsey's model. Full solutions are in the part's notes.

The reading: Charles Jones and Dietrich Vollrath's Introduction to Economic Growth, the clearest first book; Daron Acemoglu's Introduction to Modern Economic Growth and David Romer's Advanced Macroeconomics, for the graduate versions; and William Easterly's Elusive Quest for Growth, for what went wrong in practice. Then the papers, from Harrod to the frontier.

This part measured what capital can do, and found a residual it cannot explain. The next part is about the residual. In 1990 Paul Romer built a theory of growth on one property of ideas: unlike a lamp or a boat, an idea can be used by everyone at once. Part twenty-one: growth, part two. Ideas and institutions.
